definitions.meaning: The process by which green leaves use light, water and carbon dioxide to make food, releasing oxygen.
The process that breaks down food with oxygen to release energy, making carbon dioxide and water; it happens all the time.
The part of the plant that catches light: the leaf is where photosynthesis makes food.
The part of the plant that holds it up and carries water from the roots to the leaves.
The parts below the soil that drink in water for the plant.
A gas in the air that the leaf takes in as one ingredient of photosynthesis.
A gas released by the leaf in photosynthesis, and taken in when food is broken down in respiration.

mechanismSteps: Parts of a green plant: the leaf catches light, the stem holds the plant up, and the roots drink in water from the soil.
Photosynthesis: plants make their own food: light, water and carbon dioxide arrive at the leaf and become food and oxygen.
Respiration: the reverse process: food and oxygen are broken down to release energy, making carbon dioxide and water.
A common mistake: plants do not breathe? Gases move in and out of the leaf all the time, so a plant respires day and night.
objectives: Name the leaf, stem and roots and say what each part does
Explain photosynthesis using light, water, carbon dioxide, food and oxygen
Describe respiration as the reverse of photosynthesis
Explain why plants respire all the time, day and night
subject: science
title: Photosynthesis: how green plants make food

trap.explanation: Plants have no nose and no moving chest, so breathing is never seen. That hidden breathing is real respiration: Plants take in and give out gases too: they respire all the time, day and night, just like us. In the animation scene s4 the mistaken line is crossed out and gases are watched moving in and out of the leaf in the day and at night.
trap.misconception: Only animals breathe; plants do not.

workedExample: In scene s2, follow the leaf as a worked example: the leaf turns light, water and carbon dioxide into food and oxygen - sunlight arrives from above, water travels up from the roots, and carbon dioxide flows in from the air, so each ingredient can be pointed to before the food and oxygen appear.
